why: A's cells are embedded. X = Y ∪ χ(D^k) ⊆ E with Y closed, χ continuous and injective on the closed ball, and χ(z) ∈ Y ⟺ ‖z‖ = 1. For such a pair, H_*(χD, χS) → H_*(X,Y) and H_*(D,S) → H_*(X,Y) are isomorphisms, H_k(X,Y) ≅ R and H_i = 0 for i ≠ k. A also covers several disjoint embedded cells (dim H_i = number of i-cells, H_i ≅ R^m). B is excision for the abstract adjunction space Y ∪_g e^k along an arbitrary continuous g : S^{k-1} → Y (any Y, no separation axioms): the characteristic map induces H_n(e,ė) ≅ H_n(Y ∪_g e, Y), and H_n(e,ė;F) is F in degree k and 0 otherwise. A ⇒ B fails genuinely: B's characteristic map is injective on the boundary only when g is, so A's hypotheses do not apply to a general attachment (and A has no statement about quotient spaces). B ⇒ A fails as well: B gives neither the identification of an embedded X with a quotient Y ∪_g e (which needs compactness/closedness arguments) nor anything about several cells at once.
